does: Draws water out of a watery vegetable with salt before it is cooked or dressed, so that it keeps its bite and does not flood the dish.

intro.what: Salting and draining draws excess water from watery vegetables before dressing or cooking.
intro.why: It teaches you to control the liquid a vegetable contributes to the finished dish.

how: Slice or dice the vegetable and toss it with fine salt.
Leave it in a colander over a bowl until it has given up its water.
Rinse off the salt if the dish will be salted again, and press or pat the pieces dry.

cues.text: Liquid has collected under the colander, and the pieces have gone limp and glossy.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping the drying, so that the vegetable goes into the pan or the dressing still wet.
mistakes.fix: Press it gently in a cloth before you use it.

mistakes.mistake: Salting the dish as usual afterwards, so that it ends up far too salty.
mistakes.fix: Taste before you add any more salt.

quiz.question: Why salt and drain a watery vegetable?
choices: To retain all its water beneath the dressing.
To keep released water from flooding the dish.
quiz.because: Removing released water beforehand limits dilution of the pan or dressing.

quiz.question: Where should salted vegetables drain?
choices: In a sealed bowl without drainage.
In a colander over a bowl.
quiz.because: A colander separates the vegetable from water as it is released.

quiz.question: Which change shows water has been drawn out?
choices: Liquid below the colander and limp glossy pieces.
Dry rigid pieces and no collected liquid.
Wet pieces sitting in their own liquid without drainage.
quiz.because: Collected liquid and more flexible pieces show moisture leaving the vegetable.

quiz.question: The finished dish was too salty after this step. What would you change next time?
choices: Salt the dressing as heavily as usual.
Add more salt to finish drying the pieces.
quiz.because: The vegetable already carries salt, so later seasoning needs adjustment.
